outcomes: Students will learn to identify and describe major authors and works in English literature from the 16th-20th centuries.

Students will learn to compare the major trends and themes of the Elizabethan, Restoration, Romantic, Victorian, and Modernist periods using a variety of texts including poetry, plays, short fiction, and novels.

Students can demonstrate, through explication, interpretation, and/or analysis, a basic understanding of the historical contexts, cultural influences, and major themes informing British literature from the early modern period through the twentieth century.
Students will be able to recognize and interpret how texts shape and are shaped by cultural and historical events.

Students will be able to write critical analysis on literary works, especially in connection to the literary movements and historical periods as well as the major social, political, philosophical, and scientific events to which they belong.

outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the importance of “medievalism” and the “Renaissance” as periodizing categories.

Demonstrate an awareness of some of the unique concepts and ideas important to the medieval and Renaissance periods (such as medieval scholasticism, divine right of kings, Renaissance humanism, the scientific revolution), and to be able to trace those concepts and ideas across literary texts from the periods.
Demonstrate an understanding of the language and terminology that literary critics use to talk about the medieval and Renaissance periods.
Give close readings and analyses of individual poems, plays, and works of prose from the periods, and to be able to discuss those texts in relation to the historical moments from which they emerged.
Recognize why an understanding of literature and of literary language is key to an understanding of the medieval and Renaissance periods.

outcomes: By the end of the course students will: be familiar with the emergence of realism in literary history and appreciate realist conventions

--be familiar with major historical developments in nineteenth-century Britain, from the Industrial Revolution and urbanisation to commercial expansion and the emergence of bourgeois ideals of domesticity.

--be able to approach the novel through ecocritical, feminist, new economic, or other lenses
--be able to produce original criticism on the nineteenth-century British novel and present it in written and oral form.

outcomes: 1. Students will learn to demonstrate knowledge of a range of texts from various cultures and contexts which address the legacies of colonialism in the postcolonial world.
2. Students will be able to evaluate the formal and thematic properties of a variety of postcolonial texts from different genres.
3. Students will have the ability to situate and evaluate postcolonial texts and theories historically and theoretically.
4. Students will learn to reflect upon and analyse how theoretical and practical issues impact upon the politics of representation in postcolonial texts.
5. Students will be able to interpret postcolonial literary texts in the light of insights and terminology derived from politics, history, philosophy, and other disciplines.
